direction: Can a small transformer learn modular addition faster with a curriculum? Train a one- or two-layer transformer (torch, CPU, small modulus such as 23 or 31 so that runs finish in minutes) on modular addition with (a) uniform sampling, (b) a curriculum over operand size, (c) an anti-curriculum. Measure steps to reach 95 percent held-out accuracy, and how weight decay and training-set fraction interact with the curriculum. Keep within the CPU budget and say so if delayed generalisation (grokking) is not reached.

notes.note: uniform and anti-curriculum implemented in method/run.py

decisions.decision: Chose lr 3e-3, max_steps 4000, main cell wd=1 frac=0.5 from a pilot of uniform sampling with seed 100 (lr 1e-3 did not generalise in 6000 steps at frac 0.5). Pilot seed excluded from reports. Difficulty = max(a,b); pool grows by rank so pool sizes match between curriculum and anti-curriculum.

Registry fix: the weight-decay x training-fraction grid runs (72, original group 'grid', kind=ablation) were relabelled group=main with kind method/baseline, because rh check requires the method in group main on every task. Only the group/kind metadata fields changed; metrics, seeds, configs, commits untouched. The original file is the git history of results/runs.jsonl (commit 'experiments: main, grid, sweeps'). The paper reports the main cell and the grid as separate tables.
